Title: Nurturing National Unity and Progress through the Abolition of Native American Reservations

Introduction

Native American reservations, also known as Indian reservations, stand as a powerful symbol of the past for the Indigenous peoples and as a testament to the long and complex relationship between their communities and the federal government of the United States. Established through various treaties, congressional acts, executive orders, and other agreements, these areas aim to preserve the rights, sovereignty, customs, and traditions of the Indigenous tribes within their borders. While there may be arguments for continuing the existence of Native American reservations, it has become increasingly evident that the federal policy of maintaining reservations has not yielded the intended prosperous outcomes for Native Americans in terms of economic development, education, healthcare, and overall well-being. This essay aims to argue in favor of abolishing these reservations and implementing a policy of forced integration of Native American populations into mainstream American communities, highlighting the potential benefits of unity and progress.

The Detrimental Effects of Reservations

Before examining the potential advantages of integration, it is critical to scrutinize the consequences of sustained reservations and the seclusion of Native American communities. A lack of adequate prospects for education and employment stands as a prominent issue on reservations. Based on National Center for Education Statistics data, Native American high school graduation rates have consistently lagged behind those of their non-Native counterparts, and many students attending schools located on reservations experience limited resources and underfunding. Additionally, these areas often linger behind the rest of the country in terms of economic development, with the Economic Innovation Group's 2018 Distressed Communities Index highlighting that 10 out of the 15 most distressed zip codes in the United States reside within designated Native American lands. Poverty, unemployment, and reliance on federal aid programs prevail in these communities.

Furthermore, reservations have proven deficient in addressing matters of healthcare. The Indian Health Service (IHS), the primary healthcare provider for Native Americans, faces continuous budgetary constraints, which hinder it from catering to the healthcare needs of the population. Owing to these factors, the relatively isolated Native American communities endure persistent health disparities and lower life expectancy as compared to the general United States population. Alarmingly, an American Journal of Public Health study has noted a higher prevalence of chronic diseases, such as diabetes, heart disease, and obesity, among Indigenous groups.

The Benefits of Integration into Mainstream American Communities

Forced integration of Native American populations into mainstream American communities could present several benefits in addressing the dilemmas associated with reservations. Firstly, integrating Indigenous groups into the larger American population may help foster a more inclusive society, creating synergies between diverse cultures, which would then facilitate national unity. Engaging the Native American populations in the mainstream economy may also help spur economic development within these communities, offering better employment opportunities and relief from poverty.

Secondly, access to mainstream education could provide Native American youth with the chance to acquire education levels on par with their non-Native peers. Integrating schools and fostering diversity in classrooms may promote greater understanding and appreciation among all students of different cultures, values, and experiences. Such exposure has the potential to enrich the lives of all students, promoting the progress and collaboration of a more harmonious and productive society.

Lastly, dissolving reservations and incorporating Native Americans into the broader healthcare system could strengthen access to quality healthcare services for these communities. A more comprehensive and interconnected healthcare approach stands a greater chance of addressing the health disparities that have persisted within Native American communities and may result in better overall well-being for this population.

Conclusion

In light of the challenges that have emerged from reservation policies, abolishing Native American reservations and integrating these communities with the mainstream may present a more viable solution to promote national unity and progress. While one may argue that this approach may disrupt traditional customs and practices of these Indigenous groups, the potential benefits of increased access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities outweigh these concerns. Enhancing the well-being of Native American communities will not only foster a more inclusive society but also contribute to a more cohesive and united nation. As a whole, a policy of forced integration offers a compelling alternative that promises a brighter future not just for Indigenous groups but for all Americans.

Introduction

This was framed as a conferral of rights, not a loss of them.

5. Preservation of the individual Reformers of the era believed Native peoples faced a choice between extinction and assimilation, and that the latter was the only humane option. They cited declining populations from disease, war, and privation as evidence that isolation was unsustainable.
